title: Number of 1 Bits
pattern: Read the lowest bit, then shift
statement: Given a positive integer `n`, return how many `1` bits its binary representation contains (its *Hamming weight*).

example.why: 11 in binary is 1011, which contains three 1s.

idea: A number is stored as bits. `n & 1` keeps only the **lowest** bit — it is 1 exactly when the last binary digit is 1.
`n >> 1` shifts every bit one place to the right: the lowest bit drops off and the next one takes its place.
Repeat *read the lowest bit, then shift* until nothing is left (n becomes 0), adding up the bits we read.

complexity.timeWhy: One loop per binary digit of n — at most 32 for a 32-bit integer.

steps.text: Our example: **`n = 11`**. Each step runs one highlighted line of the code.
`count` will hold the number of 1 bits. In binary, 11 is `00001011`.
`n & 1` reads the **lowest bit** of n, which is 1. Add it: `count` = **1**.
Shift right by one. The bit we just counted falls off and the next bit moves into the lowest place. n is now 5 (`00000101`).
`n & 1` reads the **lowest bit** of n, which is 1. Add it: `count` = **2**.
Shift right by one. The bit we just counted falls off and the next bit moves into the lowest place. n is now 2 (`00000010`).
`n & 1` reads the **lowest bit** of n, which is 0. Add it: `count` = **2**.
Shift right by one. The bit we just counted falls off and the next bit moves into the lowest place. n is now 1 (`00000001`).
`n & 1` reads the **lowest bit** of n, which is 1. Add it: `count` = **3**.
Shift right by one. The bit we just counted falls off and the next bit moves into the lowest place. n is now 0 (`00000000`).
n is 0 — there are no bits left to read.
Done — the answer is **`3`**. 11 in binary is 1011, which contains three 1s.
